title: Induction of input-specific spine shrinkage on dendrites of rodent hippocampal CA1 neurons using two-photon glutamate uncaging
protocol: Transfer tissue culture inserts and SCM from six-well plates into 35 mm petri dishes.
Place uncovered 35 mm petri dish under the low magnification objective (10×).
Screen for EGFP transfected CA1 neurons using epifluorescence.
Mark the bottom of the petri dishes to indicate slices that have CA1 neurons with intact long apical dendrites.
Return petri dish to the cell culture incubator.
Start the perfusion system.
Dissolve 10 mg of MNI-caged glutamate by adding aCSF (1 mL) directly to the vial and rock or shake for 2-5 min until powder is completely dissolved.
Load the recirculating perfusion system and imaging chamber with aCSF containing 2.5 mM MNI-caged glutamate and 1 μM TTX.
Bubble carbogen through water prior to bubbling the aCSF bath to decrease evaporation.
Exchange the bath solution at minimum every 2.5 h.
Turn on the heating system and set the temperature at 30°C.
Cut the culture membrane around the hippocampal slice in the form of a rectangle using a scalpel blade.
Lift one corner of the membrane containing the hippocampal slice with fine tweezers.
Place the membrane with the attached hippocampal slice into the imaging chamber with recirculating aCSF.
Anchor the membrane with a bent gold wire to prevent slice movement in the imaging chamber.
Maintain the temperature of the aCSF between 29°C and 31°C.
Locate EGFP-expressing CA1 pyramidal neurons under a low magnification objective lens (10×).
Switch to a high magnification objective lens (e.g., Olympus, 60× IR, NA 1.0, WD 2.0 mm) for detailed imaging.
Select healthy EGFP-expressing CA1 pyramidal neurons using two-photon imaging with the 930 nm laser.
Choose neurons that exhibit straight and extended apical dendrites.
Exclude cells with unhealthy basal dendrites marked by blebs or other signs of damage.
Avoid selecting non-neuronal cells that are fused or show irregularities like fuzzy membranes.
Select secondary or tertiary basal dendrites located 40–80 μm from the soma and 15–45 μm below the slice surface for imaging.
Use low intensity laser power (∼ 1 mW at the sample) during screening of dendrites to prevent photobleaching and phototoxicity.
Employ higher-speed imaging mode (e.g., 256 × 256 pixels, 0.14 μm/pixel, 500 msec/frame) for imaging dendritic segments.
Ensure dendritic segments do not include blebbing and have similar fluorescence intensity and diameter in ROIs.
Select dendritic segments that include multiple well-isolated spines (> 2 μm) without filopodia and fuzzy membrane.
Select dendrites that have typical spine density.
Choose a well-isolated spine more than 2 μm from neighboring spines for input-specific stimulation.
Ensure the target spine is average or modestly larger compared to other spines in the region of interest.
Avoid selecting stubby-type spines.
Place the slice in the recirculating aCSF at least 15 min before imaging and uncaging to equilibrate the slice into the aCSF.
Choose a low frequency uncaging (LFU) protocol with either 0.3 mM Ca2+ or 2 mM Ca2+, both in 0 mM Mg2+ aCSF.
Set the two-photon uncaging laser to 720 nm and adjust power to 6-8 mW at the sample for glutamate uncaging.
Deliver 90 pulses of 1 ms pulse duration at 0.1 Hz for 0.3 mM Ca2+ protocol.
Deliver 90 pulses of 0.2 ms pulse duration at 0.1 Hz for 2 mM Ca2+ protocol.
Set the laser to 930 nm and adjust power to 1-1.2 mW at the sample for imaging.
Take a baseline z-stack of the ROI with 1 μm z-steps at -5 min and 0 min before uncaging.
Refocus and adjust laser beam parking spots between pulses.
Park the laser beam at a point ∼0.5 μm from the spine head in the direction away from the dendrite for glutamate uncaging.
Take a z-stack of the ROI with 1 μm z-steps every 5 minutes after uncaging until 40 minutes.
Change to a new slice after 2–2.5 hours and refresh the recirculating aCSF with TTX and MNI-caged glutamate after 2–3 hours.
Draw a box to select a region of interest (ROI) surrounding the stimulated and unstimulated spines on the imaged dendritic segment.
Measure integrated fluorescence intensity from the brightest slice in the z stack for each spine at each time point.
Select spines for analysis that are well-separated from the dendrite to avoid contamination.
Mark a solid box around the spine head in the brightest single Z stack image.
Identify adjacent background by marking a dashed box spanning the same distance from the dendrite as the spine head ROI.
Measure mean fluorescence intensity from both the spine head and background ROIs.
Multiply the mean fluorescence intensity of the background by the number of pixels in the spine head ROI.
Subtract this result from the integrated spine fluorescence to generate background-subtracted spine fluorescence intensity.
Normalize the background-subtracted spine fluorescence intensity signal over time by dividing each post-stimulation signal with the average pre-stimulation signal.
